\title{Does a tyre-degradation model transfer?\\
\large What public timing cannot identify, and what teams' pit stops reveal}

\author{Mohammed Reda Medjadj \\ Independent}

\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle
\linenumbers

\begin{abstract}
Race-strategy models are fitted and validated inside one championship. I ask
two validation questions of one protocol across \NClasses{} car classes in
Formula~1, WEC, IMSA and ELMS: does a fitted tyre-degradation slope predict a
season it never saw, and does a time-optimal planner stop where teams stopped?
Transfer is scored by the within-stint $R^2$, the share of the lap-to-lap change
inside a held-out stint that the fitted slope explains. First, public timing
rarely carries enough signal to answer the transfer question: inside a stint
fuel burn nearly cancels tyre wear, so even a slope stable by construction
could not reach $\TransferThreshold{}$ at \NCeilingBelowThreshold{} of
\NCeilingCircuits{} Formula~1 circuits; estimated directly, the slope varies
between races by a median \TauPubShareReml{}\% of its mean. Second, replaying
\NDecisions{} real first stops with each team's next stop held fixed, the
planner lands a median of \OosMedian{} laps \OosCi{} from the Formula~1 team
out of sample, but a rule that only balances tyre age
before the team's next stop does as well in every class. Third, the stops carry
what the fit misses. Read as an implied wear ratio, the ratio of the first
stint to the next is \ImpliedHarder{}
\ImpliedHarderCi{} when teams move to a harder compound and \ImpliedSofter{}
\ImpliedSofterCi{} when they move to a softer one, in the direction
hardness predicts for \ImpliedExpectedSide{}\% of decisions, against
\ImpliedFittedExpectedSide{}\% for the fitted slopes: teams act on a compound
difference the fitted slopes resolve only in part.
\end{abstract}

\vspace{0.6em}
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} race strategy; tyre degradation; out-of-sample
validation; motorsport analytics; Formula~1; endurance racing; pit stop
optimisation; retrospective audit

\doublespacing

\section{Introduction}

A pit stop is a decision under uncertainty with a measurable cost, and a
literature of optimisers has grown around it. This paper does not add another.
It asks two validation questions that the existing work, for understandable
reasons, mostly does not ask, and answers them with one protocol applied to four
championships.

The first question is \emph{transfer}: does a degradation slope fitted on past
seasons of a circuit predict the next season there? The second is
\emph{agreement with practice}: does a planner built on those slopes stop where
a professional pit wall stopped? The second is not a question about which plan
was faster. It measures where a model and a practice part company, and by how
much.

Three contributions come out of it.

\textbf{Transfer is mostly not measurable from public timing, and the reason is
physical.} Inside a stint, tyre age and the fuel burned advance together, so the
lap-to-lap shape a stint shows is the net of wear and fuel gain, and the two
nearly cancel. A noise ceiling, the score a slope that is stable by construction
earns against the lap noise actually present, falls below the conventional
threshold at most circuits. Estimated directly as a variance component, the
slope does move between races, by an amount the threshold cannot see.

\textbf{An audit against practice must hold the team's committed strategy
fixed.} A planner that stretches its second stint to the flag answers a
different question from a team that has already planned a second stop, and the
difference looks like a disagreement of \FoneMedian{} laps. With the team's next stop
held fixed, the planner and the team agree to within a few laps, out of sample
as well as in it. That agreement, however, comes from the horizon: a rule that
uses no fitted quantity and simply balances tyre age before the team's next stop
does as well.

\textbf{The stops carry what the fit misses.} Treating the stop as an
optimal-replacement decision, the lap a team chose implies a ratio of the new
tyre's wear rate to the old one's. That implied ratio is a ratio of stint
lengths and uses no fitted slope, and it follows compound hardness in the
direction physics predicts, in both directions of change, where the fitted
slopes are no better than chance and, given a baseline pace per compound, only
partly better: teams act on a difference between compounds that the fitted
model resolves only in part.

The modelling is simpler than much of the work cited, and it ignores energy
management. The contribution is the protocol and what it returned.

\section{Related work}

Race-strategy research is mostly about building the optimiser: discrete-event
simulation, Monte Carlo, dynamic programming, mixed-integer programming,
reinforcement learning and game theory, each used to compute a better plan than a
team would otherwise choose.

\citet{bekker2009} give the earliest sustained operations-research treatment,
simulating a full race with overtaking and traffic under the refuelling rules of
the time. \citet{heilmeier2018} introduce the lap-time decomposition much of the
later work rests on, combining fuel mass, tyre degradation and driver effects,
and \citet{heilmeier2020mc} extend it to a probabilistic simulation sampling
accidents, safety cars and lap-time variability. \citet{carrasco2022} give an
exact dynamic program over stop laps and compound choice, and \citet{aguad2024}
formulate the problem as a zero-sum feedback Stackelberg game between two
drivers. In endurance racing the same machinery has been built almost entirely
for electric cars: \citet{vankampen2022} plan stints under thermal limits,
\citet{vankampen2024} price a competitor's response by model predictive control,
and \citet{devries2026} pose the race as a two-agent game.
\citet{boettinger2023} simulate GT racing at the Nordschleife and learn a stop
policy. Recent Formula~1 work adds learning: \citet{thomas2025} apply
explainable reinforcement learning to compound and stop timing,
\citet{fieni2025} combine a mixed-integer program with an RL agent,
\citet{fieni2026} extend it to self-play, and \citet{todd2025} forecast tyre
energy from team telemetry.

\paragraph{Validation out of sample.} Several of these works validate something
on data they did not fit, and what they validate differs.
\citet{cappello2026} build a Bayesian state-space model of degradation from the
same public timing source used here and evaluate it by rolling-origin
cross-validation on 19 race sessions of one season; they also report
compound-specific degradation differences as not statistically distinct, which
is consistent with how little signal I find at scale. \citet{heilmeier2020nn}
train neural networks on the real timing of the six seasons from 2014 to 2019
to reproduce the stop decisions of top-ten finishers, and score them on held-out
races. \citet{santillana2026} calibrates a real-time Monte Carlo engine on 126
races and validates its outcome probabilities on held-out seasons, while its
degradation models are fitted per race. \citet{tulabandhula2014} forecast the
change in rank position over a pit cycle in professional stock-car racing,
validate on the later part of each race, and build a tyre-change decision
system on those forecasts. What none of them does is hold out whole seasons of a
circuit and ask whether a fitted degradation \emph{slope} predicts them, across
championships, which is the first question here.

\paragraph{Comparison with what teams did.} \citet{heilmeier2020nn} are the
closest: their networks learn to imitate real stops, so their held-out score is
a comparison with team decisions, though of an imitator rather than of an
optimiser. \citet{santillana2026} compares the stop counts its engine recommends
with the strategies teams executed. \citet{bekker2009} compare with real races
and \citet{aguad2024} compare strategic with non-strategic agents inside their
own game. What the audit here adds is lap-level: an optimiser's recommended lap
for each of a large sample of real first stops, against the lap the team chose,
with the team's committed strategy held fixed.

\paragraph{The stop as a replacement decision.} A pit stop replaces a wearing
asset at a fixed cost, which makes it an optimal-replacement problem in the
sense of \citet{rust1987}, who recovered the cost parameters a bus-fleet
manager acted on from his observed engine replacements; \citet{romer2006} asks
the same question of professional football coaches and finds them departing
from the value-maximising choice. Section~\ref{sec:implied} takes the first
step of that programme: it recovers from teams' stops the relative wear rate
they act on and compares it with the fitted one.

\paragraph{A mechanism that predicts early stops.} \citet{salminen2026} solves
the two-car one-stop game analytically and derives the earliest lap on which an
undercut cannot be answered, the only published mechanism I have found that
predicts stopping \emph{before} the time optimum. Section~\ref{sec:implied}
tests it on the same decisions.

\section{Data and protocol}

\subsection{Sources and scope}

Formula~1 lap timing, tyre compound, track status and weather come from the
FastF1 API. WEC, IMSA and ELMS timing comes from an endurance database
published on Hugging Face as \texttt{tobil/imsa} under the MIT licence; it
carries lap times, stint structure, flag state and an estimated tyre age, but
\emph{not} tyre compound. The endurance degradation models are therefore
net-slope models where the Formula~1 one is per compound. Two further Formula~1
sources serve Section~\ref{sec:repairs} only: the compounds Pirelli nominated
for each race, and second-practice laps from the OpenF1 API. Formula~1 is
modelled on the seasons before the 2026 rules throughout; the
\NRacesFoneHeldOut{} races of 2026 already ingested are held out of every model
and audit. Table~\ref{tab:scope} gives the scope and Table~\ref{tab:samples}
every decision set the results are computed on.

\midrule

\paragraph{Which laps are modelled.} A lap enters a fit only if it is a
green-flag racing lap: in-laps, out-laps, neutralised laps, laps the source
marks inaccurate or deleted and wet-compound laps are dropped, so every
coefficient is a dry-weather quantity. Laps slower than a fixed multiple
($\TrimPublished{}$) of the driver--race's own median are trimmed as traffic,
and a stint is modelled only if enough laps survive to fit a shape to. The
per-circuit counts at every stage are generated into the degradation reports.
The frame does not remove variation the filters cannot see: a driver lifting to
manage a tyre, an engine mode, a blue flag that cost less than the trim.

\subsection{The degradation model}

For driver--race $i$ and lap $\ell$, with tyre age $a$ and compound $c$,
%
\begin{equation}
y_{i\ell} \;=\; \alpha_i \;+\; \phi\,\ell \;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{d}\beta_{c,k}\,a_{i\ell}^{\,k} \;+\; \varepsilon_{i\ell},
\label{eq:degradation}
\end{equation}
%
where $y$ is lap time, $\alpha_i$ a driver--race fixed effect absorbing car,
driver and the day's conditions, and $\phi\ell$ a lap-number term carrying the
fuel burned and any steady track evolution. The degree $d \in \{1,2\}$ is chosen
per circuit by cross-validation. The fuel and wear terms are identified only
because different stints start at different laps on fresh tyres; within a stint
$a$ and $\ell$ advance together. In endurance, where cars refuel, the fuel load
resets at every stop and the two cannot be separated at all, so the model keeps
a single net slope of lap time on tyre age.

Estimation is ordinary least squares. Every published Formula~1 coefficient was
checked for estimability: deleting its column lowers the rank of the design for
all \EstChecked{} of them. Standard errors are cluster-robust (CR1) on the
driver--race and referred to $t(G-1)$ \citep{cameron2015}. Drivers in one race
also share shocks the driver--race cluster does not cover, and clustering on the
race instead leaves \RaceClusterZero{} of the \RaceClusterN{} slope intervals
containing zero rather than \RaceClusterZeroDr{}. Section~\ref{sec:variance}
estimates that race-level variation directly.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{s3_f1_degradation.png}
\caption{Linear tyre-degradation coefficients for Formula~1, by circuit and
compound, with driver--race-clustered intervals: \NCoefficientsFone{}
coefficients across \NCircuitsFone{} circuits. These intervals do not include
the variation of the slope between races, which Section~\ref{sec:variance}
measures. Points outside the plotted range are named under the axis.}
\label{fig:degradation}
\end{figure}

The model gives each compound its own wear slope but no baseline of its own:
once the driver-race intercept is removed, compounds are assumed equally fast
when new. Section~\ref{sec:implied} tests what a baseline per compound changes.

Two features of Figure~\ref{fig:degradation} matter for what follows.
\PctCoefCrossingZero{}\% of the slopes have an interval containing zero, and
within a circuit \PctCompoundOverlap{}\% of compound pairs have overlapping
intervals: the compound distinction the model carries is largely unresolved by
the data. Neither is screened out, because screening on resolved slopes would
select the circuits likeliest to transfer.

\subsection{Transfer, and what limits its measurement}
\label{sec:transfermethod}

Fit on every season of a circuit-class but one, predict the held-out season, and
score the within-stint demeaned residual:
%
\begin{equation}
R^{2}_{\text{within}} \;=\; 1 - \frac{\sum_{s}\sum_{\ell \in s}\bigl(\tilde{y}_{\ell} - \tilde{\hat{y}}_{\ell}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{s}\sum_{\ell \in s}\tilde{y}_{\ell}^{\,2}},
\qquad
\tilde{x}_{\ell} = x_{\ell} - \overline{x}_{s}.
\label{eq:transfer}
\end{equation}
%
Demeaning each stint removes the driver--race intercept, which cannot be known
for a race that has not happened, so the score tests the \emph{shape} a stint
takes. Because $a$ and $\ell$ advance together inside a stint, that shape is the
net of wear and fuel: in Formula~1, $(\beta_c + \phi)$ per lap. It is this net
quantity Result~1 is about, and its size limits what any score can show.

\paragraph{The noise ceiling.} A low score has two explanations: the slope moved
between seasons, or there was never enough signal in the laps for any slope to
be recovered. To separate them, lap times are rebuilt from each circuit's own fit
with \emph{one} degradation slope for every season, so the slope is stable by
construction, plus residuals resampled in whole stints to keep their
within-stint correlation. The residuals come from a fit that gives each season
its own slope, so real movement of the slope is not counted as noise; with
pooled-fit residuals instead the ceiling is lower by at most
\CeilingResidGapMax{} at any circuit. Running the real protocol on the rebuilt
laps gives the ceiling: the score a perfectly stable slope earns against the
noise present. A circuit is then classified by the ceiling and by the gap
between ceiling and measured score: \emph{no signal} if the ceiling is below
$\CeilingMeasurable{}$; otherwise \emph{stable} if the gap is below
$\StableGap{}$, \emph{unstable} if it exceeds $\UnstableGap{}$, and
\emph{borderline} between. Degenerate synthetic fits are excluded and named.

\paragraph{Between-race variance.} The ceiling says whether the score could
detect movement; it does not measure the movement. For that, each
circuit-compound gets one linear slope per season, each season being a single
race, with its driver--race-clustered standard error. The between-race variance
$\tau^2$ of those slopes is estimated by restricted maximum likelihood and by
the method of moments \citep{dersimonian1986}, with a Q-profile interval \citep{viechtbauer2007}, and
summarised by Cochran's $Q$ and by $I^2$, the share of the observed spread not
due to sampling error \citep{higgins2002}. Because the per-race standard errors
do not allow for shocks common to every car at the same moment of a race, $I^2$
is if anything an upper bound. The same is done for each endurance
circuit-class with its net slope.

\subsection{The planners}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{The multi-stop dynamic program.} For an endurance race of $L$ laps
with green pace $p$, net slope $\beta$, pit loss $\pi$ and fuel range $F$, a
plan is a partition of $L$ into stints $(n_1,\dots,n_{m+1})$ with $m$ stops,
of total time
%
\begin{equation}
T(n_1,\dots,n_{m+1}) \;=\; m\pi \;+\; \sum_{j}\left(n_j p + \beta\,\frac{n_j(n_j+1)}{2}\right),
\qquad n_j \le F,
\label{eq:dp}
\end{equation}
%
minimised exactly by a dynamic program in remaining laps for each $m$ from the
fuel minimum $\lceil L/F \rceil - 1$ upward. A race is \emph{tyre-limited} when
the time-optimal $m$ exceeds that minimum.

\paragraph{The Monte Carlo engine.} The single-next-stop engine evaluates every
candidate lap for the next stop over \NDraws{} shared draws. Each draw samples
the degradation and fuel coefficients from their sampling distributions ($t(G-1)$
scaled by the cluster-robust standard errors), the neutralisation rate from its
Gamma posterior, and lap noise at the cross-validated residual scale. Candidate
laps share draws, so a comparison between two laps carries no unrelated
sampling noise. A \emph{cover-aware} variant runs the audited car and one rival
under the same draws, resolves the pit exchange on the lap both have stopped,
lets a gained position survive with the circuit's measured rate of adjacent-car
swaps, and lets the rival answer each of the audited car's laps with its best
reply: a Stackelberg leader in the sense of \citet{aguad2024}, solved by
enumeration.

\subsection{The audit}
\label{sec:auditprotocol}

\paragraph{Decisions.} The engine of Section~\ref{sec:method} is the planner
audited. For every race with a fitted model, the first stop of
each of the top \NFinishers{} classified finishers in Formula~1 (\NCars{} cars
per class in endurance) is replayed. The engine is asked \LookbackFone{} laps
before the real stop in Formula~1 and \LookbackEnd{} in endurance, given the
state as it was, with rivals on their real plans. Stops before lap
\MinFirstStopFone{} (\MinFirstStopEnd{} in endurance) are excluded as incidents.
This is a replay, not a forecast: the decision point is defined by a stop that
happened.

\paragraph{The committed horizon.} The engine plans one stop. If it is allowed to
run the stint after that stop to the flag, it answers a different question from
a team that has already planned a second stop, and will stop later for that
reason alone. Every decision whose driver stopped again is therefore replayed
with the race ending, for the engine, at that driver's real next stop.
Everything after that stop runs on fresh tyres whichever first-stop lap is
chosen, so it is common to every candidate: the optimum over the shortened
horizon is the optimum given the team's own next stop. In endurance each stint
is also bounded by the fuel range. Run to the flag instead, the same engine is a
median \FoneMedian{} laps late in Formula~1; that number is a property of the
question, and Section~\ref{sec:audit} reports the committed replay.

\paragraph{Out of sample.} The circuit models are fitted on the seasons the
decisions come from. Every committed decision is therefore also replayed with
the fuel and degradation coefficients refitted on every pre-2026 season except
its own, at the published degree; a circuit raced in one season only cannot be
replayed this way and is counted out.

\paragraph{Reference rules.} With one stop before a fixed endpoint and linear
slopes, the time-optimal stop $k$ laps after the decision solves
%
\begin{equation}
\beta_{\mathrm{old}}\,(a_0 + k) \;=\; \beta_{\mathrm{new}}\,(W - k),
\label{eq:closedform}
\end{equation}
%
for a tyre aged $a_0$ and $W$ laps to the endpoint. It depends on the slopes
only through their ratio; the fuel term and any cost paid once per stop cancel.
At a ratio of one it balances tyre age either side of the stop and uses no
fitted quantity at all; I call that the \emph{ratio-one rule}. Three further
rules are scored on the decisions run to the flag: B1 divides the race into
equal stints; B2 stops when the stint's accumulated loss
$\beta\,a(a+1)/2$ first exceeds the pit loss; B3 runs the fuel load out, and is
undefined in Formula~1, which has not refuelled since 2010.

\paragraph{What the stops reveal.} Equation~\ref{eq:closedform} can be
inverted at the lap the team chose, giving the ratio
$\beta_{\mathrm{new}}/\beta_{\mathrm{old}} = (a_0+k)/(W-k)$ that would have
made that lap optimal: the age of the tyre at the stop over the length of the
stint after it. No fitted slope enters it. It is an implied parameter, which
may stand for what teams know or for what they believe, and it uses one lap per
decision. A discrete-time hazard uses every lap of
the stint instead: the probability of stopping on lap $t$, given the car is
still out, is modelled as a logistic function of the old tyre's next-lap loss
$\hat\beta_{\mathrm{old}}a_t$ and the new tyre's loss to the endpoint
$\hat\beta_{\mathrm{new}}(W-t)$, with the fitted slopes plugged in and an
indicator for a neutralised lap. The ratio of the two weights is one if teams
weigh the tyres as the fit does. Inside one stint $a_t + (W-t)$ is constant, so
the two weights are told apart only by how the fitted slopes and $W$ vary
between stints; the slopes' own noise is therefore part of what identifies the
ratio, and every bootstrap replicate refits them on the races it drew. $W$ is
the team's next stop, known only afterwards.

\paragraph{Intervals.} Every interval is a percentile bootstrap at the level the
data vary at: circuits or circuit-classes for transfer, races for the audit,
since drivers in one race share a track, a Safety Car and a tyre allocation.

\section{Result 1: transfer is mostly not measurable, and slopes do move}
\label{sec:transfer}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.86\textwidth]{r1_transfer.png}
\caption{Leave-one-season-out within-stint $R^2$, one point per endurance
circuit-class. Of \NCircuitClasses{} measured, \NTransferAboveTwo{} clear
$\TransferThreshold{}$.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

Measured as a threshold count, transfer looks rare. Of \NCircuitClasses{}
endurance circuit-classes, \NTransferAboveTwo{} clear a within-stint $R^2$
(Equation~\ref{eq:transfer}) of $\TransferThreshold{}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer}); the best is \BestTransfer{}
at \BestTransferWhere{}, and almost everywhere else a slope fitted on the other
seasons predicts the held-out one no better than that season's own mean.
Formula~1 looks the same: \NFoneAboveTwo{} of \NCeilingCircuits{} circuits clear
it. The rest of this section shows that the count is
mostly a statement about signal, not about stability.

\subsection{Why the score is low: fuel and wear cancel inside a stint}

Over the \CancelN{} Formula~1 circuits with a ceiling verdict, the median lap-number term is
\CancelFuel{}\,s per lap and the median wear slope \CancelWear{}: within a
stint the car gains almost as much from burning fuel as it loses to its tyres,
and the net slope the score has to predict has a median size of
\CancelNet{}\,s per lap of tyre age, against a median lap noise of
\CancelNoise{}\,s. At \CancelLowest{} the two
are \CancelLowestFuel{} and \CancelLowestWear{}. The size of the net slope ranks
the circuits' ceilings with a Spearman correlation of \CancelRho{}.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{r1_ceiling.png}
\caption{Measured leave-one-season-out score against the ceiling a perfectly
stable slope earns against the same lap noise. Points near the dashed diagonal
transfer as well as a stable slope could; points well below it have slopes that
move. Left of the vertical line, no slope could have cleared
$\TransferThreshold{}$.}
\label{fig:ceiling}
\end{figure}

The noise ceiling of Section~\ref{sec:transfermethod} makes this precise
(Figure~\ref{fig:ceiling}). It runs from
\CeilingLowest{} at \CeilingLowestWhere{} to \CeilingHighest{} at
\CeilingHighestWhere{}, and at \NCeilingBelowThreshold{} of
\NCeilingCircuits{} Formula~1 circuits and \EndCeilBelow{} of \EndCeilN{}
endurance circuit-classes a perfectly stable slope could not have cleared
$\TransferThreshold{}$. The threshold count therefore measures how much signal a
circuit carries at least as much as it measures stability.

Priced against its ceiling, Formula~1 has \NCeilingUnstable{} circuits whose
slopes move, \NCeilingStable{} whose slope holds, \NCeilingNoSignal{} with no
recoverable signal and \NCeilingBorderline{} borderline. The endurance classes
divide differently: \EndCeilNoSignal{} with no signal, \EndCeilStable{} stable,
\EndCeilBorderline{} borderline and \EndCeilUnstable{} unstable. Whether that
contrast belongs to the championships or to the model, which carries a slope
per compound in Formula~1 and one net slope in endurance, these data cannot
say.

\subsection{How much the slope moves between races}
\label{sec:variance}

The ceiling tells whether the score could have seen movement; the variance
components measure it, on the linear form of Equation~\ref{eq:degradation}
fitted to one season at a time. Over \VarN{} Formula~1 circuit-compounds with at least
three seasons, Cochran's $Q$ rejects a common slope at \VarHet{} of them, and the median
$I^2$ is \VarIsq{} \VarIsqCi{}: most of the spread between seasons is not
sampling error. The between-race standard deviation is a median
\TauPubShareReml{}\% \TauPubShareRemlCi{} of the circuit-compound's mean slope
by restricted maximum likelihood (REML), \VarTauShare{}\% by the moment
estimator, which runs low with three or four seasons, and its interval excludes
zero at \VarTauExcl{} of \VarN{}. Estimated as one relative standard deviation
common to the \TauPubCommonN{} circuit-compounds whose mean is resolved from
zero, in a hierarchical model with one mean each, it is \TauPubCommon{}\%
\TauPubCommonCi{}. $I^2$ is highest where the ceiling verdict says
unstable (median \VarIsqUnstable{}) and lowest where there is no signal
(\VarIsqNoSignal{}), so the two measures agree where both can speak. In
endurance, $Q$ rejects at \EndVarHet{} of \EndVarN{} circuit-classes with a
median $I^2$ of \EndVarIsq{}, including \EndVarIsqStable{} among those the
ceiling calls stable. Slopes move between races nearly everywhere; at most
circuits the within-stint score is simply too weak an instrument to notice.

Three objections do not change this. \emph{Compound labels}: coded by the real
compound each lap ran on, $Q$ rejects at \TauRealHet{} of \TauRealN{} and the
median share is \TauRealShareReml{}\% \TauRealShareRemlCi{}; at the
\TauUnchangedCircuits{} circuits whose nomination never changed, at
\TauUnchangedHet{} of \TauUnchangedN{}, with a median of
\TauUnchangedShareReml{}\% \TauUnchangedShareRemlCi{}. A change of rubber is
not what moves the slope. \emph{Net slope}: season by season, the wear slope and
the lap-number term trade off against each other, so the quantity the score
actually measures is their sum, estimated directly by writing
$\phi\ell + \beta a = \phi(\ell - a) + (\beta + \phi)a$. It moves more: $Q$
rejects at \TauNetHet{} of \TauNetN{}, with a median $I^2$ of \TauNetIsq{} and
a between-race standard deviation of \TauNetShareReml{}\% \TauNetShareRemlCi{}
of its mean. \emph{Estimator}: the shares above are REML; the moment estimator
gives lower values (\TauPubShareDl{}\% for the published coding,
\TauNetShareDl{}\% for the net slope), as it should with three or four seasons.

\paragraph{Track temperature.} The first candidate cause is the track. Regressing
the season slopes on the race's median track temperature, with one intercept
per circuit-compound, gives \TempTheta{}\,s per lap per ten degrees (standard
error \TempThetaSe{}), against a median within-circuit range of \TempRange{}
degrees between seasons. The effect is real and small: it removes
\TempShare{}\% of the between-race variance.

This variance also bears on the audit. The random-effects standard error of a
circuit-compound's mean slope, which counts the between-race variation, is a
median \VarSeInflation{} times the driver--race-clustered one the engine draws
from, and up to \VarSeInflationMax{} times. Section~\ref{sec:audit} reruns the
audit with the wider distributions.

\subsection{Repairs a team would try}
\label{sec:repairs}

\paragraph{Code the tyre by what it was.} Compound labels are relative: Pirelli
nominates three of its compounds for each race, so the same circuit's Medium
can be a different rubber from one season to the next. I collected the
nomination for all \NAllocationRaces{} races from 2022 to 2025 from the race
articles of Wikipedia, checked against Pirelli's press releases where they state
it in text (\NAllocationPirelli{} races, agreeing every time), and recoded every
lap. Where the allocation changed, at \NCompoundChanged{} circuits with a
ceiling verdict, the median score moves from \CompoundRelative{} to
\CompoundReal{}, a paired difference of \CompoundDiff{} \CompoundDiffCi{}, better
at \NCompoundBetter{} circuits and worse at \NCompoundWorse{}. Recoding gives
each real compound fewer seasons than its relative label had, and does not
repair transfer.

\paragraph{Measure it on Friday.} In second practice every car runs long runs on
that weekend's tyres and asphalt. Used in place of other seasons, the Friday
slope scores \FridayRaw{} against \FridayOther{}, worse in
\NFridayRawWorse{} of \NFridayRaces{} races, a paired difference of
\FridayRawDiff{} \FridayRawDiffCi{}. Friday runs degrade faster than the race by
a median \FridayOffset{}\,s per lap; removing that offset, learned on the other
circuits, still leaves \FridayCorrected{}.

\paragraph{Price the temperature.} Adding tyre age times track temperature to
each circuit's own model, with the held-out race's temperature, changes the score
by a median \TempOwnDiff{} \TempOwnDiffCi{}: three training races cannot pin
down a temperature sensitivity. Borrowing the sensitivity from the other
circuits instead changes it by \TempCatDiff{} \TempCatDiffCi{}, better at
\TempCatBetter{} of \TempN{} circuits, too little to establish.

\paragraph{Baselines.} Predicting each season only from earlier ones, the
question a team actually faces, costs a median \BasePastDiff{}
\BasePastDiffCi{} against leave-one-season-out. A slope common to the category,
the median of every other circuit's fit, scores \BaseCategoryDiff{}
\BaseCategoryDiffCi{} against the circuit's own: over all circuits a circuit's
history does not measurably beat a slope that knows nothing about it. At the
\CeilingShareN{} circuits whose ceiling exceeds $\CeilingMeasurable{}$, the
circuit's own slope recovers a median \CeilingShareMedian{} of its ceiling
against \CeilingShareCategory{} for the category slope, a difference of
\CeilingCategoryDiff{} \CeilingCategoryDiffCi{} that is not established either.
Refitted with the traffic trim at $\TrimLow{}$ or $\TrimHigh{}$ instead of
$\TrimPublished{}$, at most \TrimShareMoved{}\% of slopes move by more than a
tenth and the median score ranges from \TrimLoroLow{} to \TrimLoroHigh{}: the
low scores are sensitive to the trim, and no setting brings them near the
threshold.

\subsection{Car type}

Grouped by car type, the raw scores favour GT3 classes, \GTThreeMean{} against
\ProtoMean{} for prototypes, a difference of \TransferDiff{}
\TransferDiffCI{} with a permutation $p$ of \TransferP{}. That comparison treats
classes at different events as exchangeable, and they are not: the two
highest GT3 scores, both at Lime Rock, come from an event with no prototype
class. Paired within the
\GtPairEvents{} events that run both, GT3 scores higher by \GtPairDiff{}
\GtPairDiffCi{}, at \GtPairHigher{} of them, with an exact sign-flip $p$ of
\GtPairP{}. The raw difference is mostly a difference between circuits, and I do
not claim one between car types. For the same reason the near-specification
ELMS LMP2 field cannot speak to Balance of Performance: at \NLmptwoNoSignal{}
of its \NLmptwoTotal{} circuits its laps carry no recoverable signal.

\section{A note on the endurance planner}
\label{sec:regime}

The dynamic program of Equation~\ref{eq:dp} also reports, for each endurance
race, whether the tyre-optimal plan needs more stops than the fuel minimum:
\NTyreLimited{} of \NRaceSeasons{} race-seasons do. The regime is decided inside
the planner by weighing an extra stop against what the tyre gives back, so it is
close to an identity of the model and is reported here only as a description of
where these championships sit. Ranked by pit loss alone the race-seasons
separate at an AUC of \RegimeAucPitLoss{} \RegimeAucPitLossCI{}, by the net slope
alone at \RegimeAucSlope{} \RegimeAucSlopeCI{}; dropping either from the
planner's own index, $\log\beta + 2\log n - \log\pi$, costs a similar amount
(\IndexDropDiff{} \IndexDropDiffCi{}), so both set the regime. Refuelling is a
median \RefuelShare{}\% of the stop loss and does not change the count, and no
tyre-limited race-season has a pit loss above \CheapStopEdge{}\,s, an edge set by
one race. Figure~\ref{fig:pitloss} in the Appendix shows the class-level
relation ($r = \PitLossR{}$ on six class points). The decision endurance teams
more often face, whether to change tyres at a fuel stop, is not in the model
(Section~\ref{sec:threats}).

\section{Result 2: with the strategy held fixed, the planner agrees with teams, and the agreement comes from the horizon}
\label{sec:audit}

The planner chooses the lap of the next stop to minimise one car's expected race
time, on the decisions and horizons of Section~\ref{sec:auditprotocol}. It
represents neither the tyre allocation, nor traffic, nor energy management,
nor a championship position. Every number below measures a
disagreement between a model and a practice, not which was faster.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{r3_audit_bias.png}
\caption{Model lap minus team lap over the \NDecisions{} replayed first stops.
Grey: the engine run to the flag. Colour: the same decisions with the stint
ending at the team's own next stop; in endurance only decisions with a later
stop can be replayed. Boxes show quartiles.}
\label{fig:audit}
\end{figure}

\subsection{The agreement}
\label{sec:committed}

With each team's next stop held fixed, the planner lands a median of
\CommitAllAfter{} laps \CommitAllCi{} from the real stop over the \NCommitAll{}
replayable Formula~1 decisions, against \CommitAllBefore{} when the same
decisions are run to the flag (Figure~\ref{fig:audit}). In endurance the
interval contains zero in all \NEndCommitContainsZero{} classes.

The agreement survives the checks a reader would ask for first.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Out of sample.} With slopes fitted without the decision's season, the
median is \OosMedian{} \OosCi{} over \OosN{} decisions, against
\OosPublished{} in sample on the same ones; the recommended lap moves for
\OosMoved{}\% of decisions, by a median of \OosShift{} lap.
\item \emph{Wider uncertainty.} With every slope's sampling distribution widened
to its random-effects standard error, the median is \WideMedian{} \WideCi{}.
\item \emph{Design.} Asked ten or fifteen laps ahead instead of five, and on every
finisher instead of the top five, the median runs from \DesignMinMedian{} to
\DesignMaxMedian{} across six designs.
\item \emph{Green flag only.} On the \FoneGreenN{} decisions whose real stop was
under green, it is \FoneGreenMedian{} \FoneGreenCi{}; keeping only decisions
whose \emph{next} stop was under green, \CommitGreenAfter{} \CommitGreenCi{}.
In IMSA, where \ImsaCautionMin{} to \ImsaCautionMax{}\% of first stops are
taken under caution, the green-flag medians are \ImsaGtpGreenMedian{},
\ImsaGtdGreenMedian{} and \ImsaGtdproGreenMedian{} for GTP, GTD and GTD PRO.
\item \emph{Not a narrow window.} In Formula~1 races with a second stop, the
window between the decision and that stop is a median \CommitWindow{} laps; a
lap drawn uniformly inside it would miss the real stop by a median
\CommitUniformMiss{} and the window's midpoint by \CommitMidpointMiss{},
against \CommitEngineMiss{} for the engine on the same decisions. In endurance
the engine beats both only in the \NEndCommitInformative{} IMSA classes; in WEC
Hypercar and ELMS the fuel range leaves \EndCommitWecHypercarWindow{} to
\EndCommitElmsLmptwoProAmWindow{} laps and the replay is uninformative.
\end{itemize}

Conditioning on the team's next stop is conditioning on a later decision, made
knowing where the first stop had been. The committed median is agreement given
the plan the team revealed, which is what makes the planner and the team answer
the same question; it is not a measure of how good the planner is.

\subsection{Where the agreement comes from}
\label{sec:designchecks}

Equation~\ref{eq:closedform} describes what the engine is doing: it lands a
median of \ClosedFormGap{} laps from the engine's own lap on \ClosedFormN{}
decisions at linear circuits. Its ratio-one form, which uses no fitted quantity,
is the natural reference, and it ties the engine's median absolute error in
\RatioOneTies{} of \RatioOneClasses{} classes (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The
agreement of the committed replay is therefore produced by the horizon: once
the team's next stop is known, balancing tyre age before it is as close to
practice as the full engine. On this measure the Monte Carlo, the
neutralisation hazard and the fitted slopes add nothing to the agreement.

In endurance this is forced. The model has one net slope, so
$\beta_{\mathrm{old}} = \beta_{\mathrm{new}}$, the timing reduces to equal tyre
ages either side of the stop whatever the slope is, and the replay tests the
fuel and neutralisation logic rather than the tyre model.

Run to the flag, a rule of thumb sits closer to practice than the optimiser in
\NClassesRuleWins{} of \NClassesScored{} classes, and in \NClassesBoneWins{} of

the optimiser is closer than every rule in \NClassesCommitBeatsRules{} classes
and ties the best in \NClassesCommitTiesRules{}, but the ratio-one rule, given
the same next stop, does as well. The rules' advantage over the optimiser run
to the flag came from the question that optimiser was asked.

\subsection{The residual}
\label{sec:residual}

What remains is concentrated in one-stop races, where the planner and the team
were always answering the same question: \CommitOneAfter{} laps
\CommitOneCi{} over \NCommitOne{} decisions, \OosOneMedian{} \OosOneCi{} out of
sample. Part of it belongs to the audit's window. Asked five laps before the
stop, the planner can be at most four laps early and arbitrarily late, and
\DesignTopFiveBound{}\% of committed decisions sit on that bound; replayed for
every finisher fifteen laps ahead, the one-stop median is
\DesignAllFifteenOneMedian{} \DesignAllFifteenOneCi{}. Part belongs to
extrapolation: \ExtrapOne{}\% of one-stop recommendations stop at a tyre age
beyond the 95th percentile of the stints observed on that compound at that
circuit, where the linear slope is no longer measured, and where the
recommendation stays inside that range the one-stop median is
\ExtrapOneInsideGap{}. What it costs is taken up in
Section~\ref{sec:deviationcost}.

\subsection{What the stops reveal}
\label{sec:implied}

The residual has a form that does not depend on the window. Inverting
Equation~\ref{eq:closedform} at the lap each team chose, over the \ImpliedN{}
decisions between two different compounds at linear circuits, gives a median
ratio $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}/\beta_{\mathrm{old}}$ of \ImpliedRatio{}
\ImpliedRatioCi{} against \ImpliedFitted{} fitted. Because the implied ratio is
$(a_0+k)/(W-k)$, this says first that teams' first stints are shorter than the
stints that follow them; the fitted value it is compared with is a ratio the
fits do not resolve, since \PctCompoundOverlap{}\% of compound pairs overlap.

The direction of the change separates the two readings. If teams act on a
difference between compounds that the fits miss, the implied ratio should fall
below one when they move to a harder compound and rise above one when they move
to a softer one; if something else shortens first stints, it should fall below
one either way. It splits by hardness (Table~\ref{tab:direction}): to a harder
compound the implied ratio is \ImpliedHarder{} \ImpliedHarderCi{} over
\ImpliedHarderN{} decisions, to a softer one \ImpliedSofter{}
\ImpliedSofterCi{} over \ImpliedSofterN{} decisions in \ImpliedSofterRaces{}
races, and it lies on the side of one that hardness predicts for
\ImpliedExpectedSide{}\% of decisions. The fitted ratios do so for
\ImpliedFittedExpectedSide{}\%, no better than a coin: they put the harder
compound at \ImpliedFittedHarder{} of the softer one's wear and the softer at
\ImpliedFittedSofter{} of the harder one's. The implied ratio therefore measures
what the fit does not resolve: teams stop as if they know which compound lasts,
and by how much, and the published fit does not show it. Part of this is the same knowledge
exercised the other way round, choosing the harder compound for the longer
stint, which the inversion cannot tell from a wear rate. The pooled
\ImpliedRatio{} is mostly the harder-compound case, which is the common one.

Part of what the fit misses is its own specification. Refitted with one
baseline pace per compound, the harder compound is slower when new, by
\OffsetHarder{}\,s \OffsetHarderCi{} over the decisions that move to it, and
the refitted slopes order the compounds on the expected side for
\OffsetsFittedSide{}\% of decisions instead of \ImpliedFittedExpectedSide{}\%:
better than chance, still short of the teams. With those baselines in the
time-optimal single stop, the planner's lap moves from \OffsetsGapPlain{} to
\OffsetsGap{} laps \OffsetsGapCi{} of the team's, so the shorter first stints
remain.

\centering
\caption{Implied and fitted ratios $\beta_{\mathrm{new}}/\beta_{\mathrm{old}}$
by the direction of the compound change, Formula~1 decisions between two
different compounds at linear circuits. Intervals resample races.}
\label{tab:direction}
\begin{tabular}{lrrll}
\toprule
Change & Decisions & Races & Implied ratio & Fitted ratio \\
\midrule
To a harder compound & \ImpliedHarderN{} & \ImpliedHarderRaces{} & \ImpliedHarder{} \ImpliedHarderCi{} & \ImpliedFittedHarder{} \ImpliedFittedHarderCi{} \\
To a softer compound & \ImpliedSofterN{} & \ImpliedSofterRaces{} & \ImpliedSofter{} \ImpliedSofterCi{} & \ImpliedFittedSofter{} \ImpliedFittedSofterCi{} \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The stop hazard, fitted on all \HazardLaps{} laps those \HazardStints{} first
stints were at risk, puts the weight teams give the new tyre's fitted loss,
relative to the old tyre's, at \HazardRatio{} \HazardRatioCi{} with the slopes
refitted in every replicate (\HazardRatioCiFixed{} if they are held fixed). It
agrees with the implied ratio in sign, not in size, and it cannot separate the
two directions: \HazardHarder{} \HazardHarderCi{} to a harder compound,
\HazardSofter{} \HazardSofterCi{} to a softer one. Since it is identified only
across stints, through slopes that do not resolve the compounds and an endpoint
known only afterwards, I read it as consistent with the implied ratio rather
than as a second measurement of it.

Compound knowledge is not the only thing the implied parameter can absorb:
wear that accelerates late in a stint, the value of keeping the option of a
Safety Car and tyre management to a planned stint length all act on the
same ratio. Five further mechanisms I could test do not account for the
shorter first stints:
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Wear that grows with fuel load.} A term in tyre age times lap number
has mixed sign, positive at \InterPositive{} of \InterN{} circuits, and
rerunning Equation~\ref{eq:closedform} with it moves the median gap from
\InterGapWithout{} to \InterGapWith{} laps, away from the real stop.
\item \emph{Heavier first stints.} Fitted separately, first-stint slopes are
steeper than later ones at only \FirstSteeper{} of \FirstPairs{}
circuit-compounds, and of the \FirstSig{} differences that are significant,
\FirstSigSteeper{} go that way; using them moves the gap from
\FirstGapPooled{} to \FirstGapSplit{} laps, again away.
\item \emph{Track position.} The cover-aware engine moves the recommendation
closer to the real stop on \RetestCloser{} of the \NRetest{} one-stop
decisions and further on \RetestFurther{}, and under each of the
\NRetestRules{} rival rules below it moves closer on at most
\RetestCloserMax{} (sign test $p \le \RetestSignPMax{}$).
\item \emph{The earliest undefendable undercut} of \citet{salminen2026}, with
the position-keeping defence, predicts no undefendable undercut before the
flag on \NRetestEuuAfterFlag{} of the \NRetestPredicted{} one-stop decisions
carrying a prediction. On the \NRetestEuuInside{} where its lap falls inside
the race, its absolute error exceeds the single-car optimiser's by a median
\RetestEuuInsideAbsDiff{} laps \RetestEuuInsideAbsDiffCi{}, closer on
\RetestEuuInsideCloser{} and further on \RetestEuuInsideFurther{}. Across all
Formula~1 decisions, for it to reproduce what teams do, tyres would have to wear
at a median \DOneImpliedTheta{}\,s per lap, \DOneThetaRatio{} times the
measured rate.
\item \emph{A gain at the stop.} With the number of stops fixed, any time
gained or lost once per stop is common to every candidate lap and cancels;
it cannot move the lap. The data show such a term with the opposite sign
anyway: laps on a new set come in slower than the fit expects, which is tyre
warm-up.
\end{itemize}
A slope biased toward durability would act in the right direction; against an
independent lap history in the Ergast schema, distributed on Kaggle, which
separates wear from fuel by a different method, the median paired difference
over \CrossSourceN{} circuits is \CrossSourceDiff{}\,s per lap against a median
wear slope of \CrossSourceWear{}. A full structural estimate in the manner of
\citet{rust1987}, with the compound difference as a parameter rather than a
fitted input, is where explaining the ratio would start.

\subsection{What the residual costs}
\label{sec:deviationcost}

The planner prices the residual at tenths of a second. Over the same stretch of
each real race, from the decision to the next stop or the flag, with
neutralised windows dropped, I compared each car's elapsed time with what its own
median green lap predicts, within races and controlling for the window's length.
Over \NDeviationCars{} first stops in \NDeviationRaces{} races, each lap of
distance from the planner's lap goes with \DeviationPerLap{}\,s of extra time
\DeviationPerLapCi{}, against \DeviationPlannerPerLap{}\,s by the planner's
own pricing. Between cars of one race the excess time has a median standard
deviation of \DeviationSpread{}\,s, so the smallest per-lap cost these decisions
could detect with 80\% power is about \DeviationMde{}\,s, and detecting the
planner's own price would take about \DeviationNeeded{} decisions. This is an
association between cars, open to every reason a team had for its lap.

\subsection{Which car is the rival}
\label{sec:rivalchoice}

A competition-aware model needs a rival, and the timing does not name one. The
published replay pairs each car with its nearest neighbour on classified
position, which, as Charles Thraves pointed out, picks the car ahead on some
decisions and the car behind on others. Against it I ran his proposal (the car
whose standalone optimal race time is closest), the car ahead on the clock that
the model of \citet{salminen2026} is defined on, and every car within one pit
loss. Over the \NRivalAllApply{} decisions where all \NRivalRules{} apply, they
name the same car \NRivalAllAgree{} times; pairwise, two rules agree on between
\RivalPairMin{}\% and \RivalPairMax{}\% of decisions, a median of
\RivalPairMedian{}\%. The recommendation barely moves between them: the
cover-aware engine stays later than the real stop under every rule. The
game-theoretic literature is built on a two-car abstraction
\citep{aguad2024,devries2026,salminen2026}; measured against real decisions,
which two cars those are is under-determined.

\section{Threats to validity}
\label{sec:threats}

\paragraph{The committed horizon is hindsight.} The replay of
Section~\ref{sec:committed} is given the team's next stop. Restricting to green-flag next stops removes the opportunistic ones,
not a plan revised during the race.

\paragraph{The endurance tyre clock.} Endurance teams often double-stint tyres,
and the decision they face is often whether to change tyres at a fuel stop. The
endurance model counts tyre age from the source's estimate, carries one net
slope with no compound, and does not represent that decision; its
tyre-limited regime answers a question endurance teams rarely ask, and its
replay cannot test the tyre model (Section~\ref{sec:designchecks}).

\paragraph{Slopes depend on the strategy.} A driver told to make a set last
drives it more gently, so a fitted slope depends partly on the stint the team
chose, which pushes in the direction of the one-stop residual and would show up
between seasons as instability. Public timing cannot remove it.

\paragraph{Reuse, not refitting.} As Giona Fieni put it, a model-based policy
retunes its degradation curves for each car and circuit and never depends on a
slope transferring. Result~1 bounds approaches that carry fitted parameters
forward (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}); for a design that refits as a matter of
course it is an argument for refitting.

\paragraph{Decided after seeing the data.} The committed replay, the rival
correction, the design checks and the analyses of Sections~\ref{sec:variance},
\ref{sec:residual} and \ref{sec:implied}, including the split of the implied
ratio by direction, were all built after the run-to-flag gap was seen. The protection against a forking path is a test the analysis could not
have seen, frozen in Section~\ref{sec:prospective}.

\paragraph{Withdrawn estimators and thin constants.} A piecewise race-time basis
meant to absorb track evolution was withdrawn after failing on real fields,
whose median identifiability of \NIdentifiability{} sits outside the range it
was shown to work in. The best endurance transfer scores rest on two or three
folds each. Both are documented in the repository.

\section{Reproducibility and a prospective test}
\label{sec:reproducibility}

Every artifact derived from committed data is regenerated by continuous
integration, which fails on any difference between the working tree and the
repository. Every number in this manuscript is a macro generated from the
committed artifacts; the source contains no digits of its own. The state the
results were computed from is archived on Zenodo, at
\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22726130}.
The repository does not redistribute the two third-party exports, both
downloaded from Kaggle, that \NBlockedLayers{} of its layers read: a Formula~1
history in the Ergast schema (lap times, pit stops, results) and a WEC results
table. Those layers cannot be regenerated from a clone; their outputs are
committed, and the only published result resting on them is the cross-source
slope check of Section~\ref{sec:implied}.

\paragraph{A prospective test, frozen before its data exist.}
\label{sec:prospective}
The committed replay --- planner, seeds, lookback, selection of cars and horizon
--- is frozen in \texttt{paper/prospective\_protocol.md}, committed before the
Formula~1 races it will be scored on had been run, with its hypotheses and
prediction intervals stated in advance: a committed median inside
\ProspectivePiSeason{} laps over the next full season, and, as a secondary test
on the races left in the current season, inside \ProspectivePiFour{}. Two
hypotheses added before the first of those races do not depend on the lookback:
the whole field replayed fifteen laps ahead, and the implied ratio. The frozen
models were fitted on cars built to the previous rules, so the test also asks
whether the replay survives a rule change. The result will be reported against
the dated file whichever way it falls. Hypothesis five freezes the pooled
implied ratio, whose value depends on how many changes go to a harder compound;
the split of Table~\ref{tab:direction} came after the freeze and is not part
of it.

\paragraph{The 2026 races already ingested.} The \HeldIngested{} Grands Prix of
2026 already in the repository were ingested before the test was frozen and are held out of every model in
this paper. The audit had never been run on them; their laps did enter an early
version of the noise ceiling, before it was restricted to 2022--2025. Replayed
with the frozen models, out of sample but \emph{not} pre-registered, the
\HeldRaces{} with a replayable decision give a committed median of
\HeldMedian{} laps \HeldCi{} over \HeldN{} decisions, \HeldWideMedian{}
\HeldWideCi{} for the whole field fifteen laps ahead over \HeldWideN{}
decisions, and an implied ratio of \HeldImplied{} \HeldImpliedCi{} over
\HeldImpliedN{} decisions, all of them to a harder compound, against
\ImpliedHarder{} for that direction in 2022--2025. The committed agreement
survives the change of rules. The implied ratio sits closer to one on the new
cars and tyres, but over \HeldImpliedN{} decisions its interval reaches the
2022--2025 value, so no change is established.

\section{Conclusion}

Public timing rarely carries enough signal to say whether a degradation slope
transfers, and the reason is physical: inside a stint the fuel burned nearly
cancels the tyre's wear, so the shape a stint shows is small against the lap
noise. Measured directly, the slope moves between races nearly everywhere, by a
median \TauPubShareReml{}\% of its mean, and by about its own size for the net
slope a stint shows; neither a change of compound nor track temperature
explains much of it. Held to the team's committed strategy, and out of sample,
a time-optimal planner stops within a few laps of the pit wall, but so does a
rule that only balances tyre age before the team's next stop: the agreement is
a property of the horizon. What the stops do reveal is the compound difference
the fit misses. Read as an implied wear ratio, the length of a team's first
stint against the next follows compound hardness in both directions of change,
where the fitted slopes are no better than chance, and only partly better once each compound has its own
baseline pace. Teams act as if they know which tyre lasts; public timing, as
modelled here, shows it only in part.

\section*{Data and code availability}

Every quantity in this paper is derived from committed artifacts by scripts in
a public repository (Section~\ref{sec:reproducibility}), which also contains the data, the figures and the tests:
\url{https://github.com/mohammedmedjadj/Motorsport-Strategy-Lab}. The state the
results were computed from is archived at
\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22726130}.

\section*{Acknowledgements}

Several researchers replied to cold emails about this work, and their replies
changed it. Charles Thraves (Universidad de Chile) identified the
rival-selection defect and proposed the standalone-time rule of
Section~\ref{sec:rivalchoice}, and named the endogeneity that bounds it. Wytze de
Vries (TU Eindhoven) raised two measurement objections to the endurance regime of
Section~\ref{sec:regime}, that class
medians pool stops with and without a driver change and that part of the
correlation may run backwards; both were tested, and neither disturbs the class
ordering. Jorn van Kampen (TU Eindhoven) described the same structure from
electric endurance racing, where a tyre change is negligible beside the charging
stop. Giona Fieni (ETH Z\"urich) drew the line between reused parameters and
model-based policy stated in Section~\ref{sec:threats}. Felipe Carrasco Heine
pointed out that the lap-time model has no baseline pace per compound, which
Section~\ref{sec:implied} tests. None of them is responsible for what this
manuscript says.
